Weight-sharing interference in this context asks: when you train separate LoRA adapters for different tasks and then merge them into one base model, do the low-rank updates reinforce, cancel, or corrupt each other — and does domain skew in the fine-tuning data make this systematically worse? The key concepts are LoRA's factored update structure (ΔW = BA, where B and A are low-rank matrices), the additive merge assumption (that you can simply sum adapter updates into the base weights), and domain skew — meaning one task's fine-tuning corpus dominates in volume, vocabulary, or distributional character. The beginner thinks interference is just "forgetting," like catastrophic forgetting in sequential fine-tuning, but the expert worries about something subtler: because LoRA constrains updates to a low-rank subspace, two adapters targeting overlapping subspaces will project their updates onto shared directions in weight space, and the resulting merged vector may satisfy neither task's objective even when neither adapter alone looked problematic. Domain skew compounds this because the dominant-domain adapter carves out a larger, more entrenched subspace, leaving the minority-domain adapter's updates with less orthogonal room — so the interference is asymmetric, not just noisy. The expert also watches for rank collapse in the merged model: the effective rank of the combined ΔW can be lower than either adapter alone if their low-rank factors partially cancel, producing a merged model that is confidently wrong in structured, reproducible ways rather than randomly degraded.

For zero interference under additive merging, the row spaces of the two update matrices ΔW₁ = B₁A₁ and ΔW₂ = B₂A₂ must be orthogonal — meaning the column space of B₁ must be orthogonal to the column space of B₂, and equivalently the row space of A₁ orthogonal to that of A₂, so that their sum ΔW₁ + ΔW₂ affects strictly non-overlapping directions in the weight space and neither update distorts the other's output. In practice this requires that the gradient signals driving each adapter during training explore disjoint subspaces of the full weight matrix, which would demand the two tasks activate entirely different neurons and attention heads — something that never happens because pretrained transformers develop highly reused, polysemantic representations where the same mid-layer heads process syntax, coreference, and domain-general semantics simultaneously across wildly different tasks. Empirically, Yadav et al. LoRA makes this worse, not better: because rank is typically set to 4–64 (far below the ambient dimension of thousands), the adapter is forced to concentrate its update into a small subspace, and two adapters trained on related-but-skewed domains will almost inevitably select overlapping high-variance directions because those directions are where the pretrained model's representations are already richest and most informative. Domain skew sharpens the asymmetry — the majority-domain adapter's B matrix columns will align with high-singular-value directions of the pretrained weight matrix, and the minority adapter, trained with weaker gradient signal, will tend to find nearby directions rather than genuinely orthogonal ones, since gradient descent has no explicit orthogonality pressure.

The intuitive answer — give the minority-domain adapter more rank to compensate for weaker gradient signal — is wrong in the merging setting, and getting this wrong is a common expert-level mistake. Once gradient signal is equalized, a lower rank for the minority adapter is often better because it forces the adapter to concentrate its update into the single highest-variance direction available to it in the residual subspace, producing a cleaner, more mergeable update — empirically, in domain-skewed instruction tuning experiments, minority-task adapters with rank 4–8 after equalization outperform rank 32–64 adapters trained under skew, because the high-rank versions overfit to minority-corpus noise and produce conflicting merge directions.

A second signature is the magnitude-weighted sign conflict rate: for each element of ΔW₁ and ΔW₂, check whether they have opposite signs, and weight each conflict by the product of their magnitudes — this is exactly the TIES-Merging diagnostic, and empirically a magnitude-weighted conflict rate above ~40% in the top percentile of parameters predicts merge degradation of more than 3 accuracy points on the minority task with reasonable reliability. Rank deficiency in the merged update represents genuinely destroyed information in the sense that the canceled directions are gone from ΔW_merged, but the base model's own representations in those directions are still intact — so post-merge fine-tuning isn't reconstructing lost information from nothing, it's re-learning which base model directions to activate for each task, which is a much easier optimization problem than the original fine-tuning and explains why even 100–500 steps of post-merge tuning recovers surprisingly large fractions of lost performance. The most efficient data regime is a balanced mixture of both domains regardless of original skew — this is counterintuitive because you might think you only need minority-domain data to fix minority-task degradation, but the rank-deficient directions were shared between tasks, so single-domain recovery fine-tuning tends to re-introduce the original interference pattern by pushing the merged model back toward one adapter's subspace; balanced data forces the recovery to find directions that serve both tasks simultaneously. For the objective, knowledge distillation from the individual pre-merge adapters is substantially more efficient than standard cross-entropy on labels: you run the merged model and each original adapter on the same inputs, minimize KL divergence between their output distributions, and the adapter logits provide a much richer signal about which directions need recovery than hard labels do — Gu et al.'s work on model merging with distillation (2024) showed 2–4x sample efficiency improvement over label-based recovery fine-tuning. For parameter scope, the critical finding is that recovery fine-tuning should not touch the full merged weight matrix — instead, add a fresh low-rank adapter on top of the merged model and train only that, because modifying the merged weights directly risks re-introducing interference in the directions that merged cleanly, while a new adapter can surgically fill in the rank-deficient subspace without disturbing what the merge got right. Practically, 200–500 steps with rank-4 to rank-8 recovery adapters on balanced distillation data recovers 70–85% of the performance gap caused by rank deficiency, with diminishing returns beyond that point because the remaining gap reflects true information loss from cancellation that no amount of fine-tuning on the available data can reconstruct without access to the original training signal.
